Before the pair or group work in Chapter 8, did you ask “How many freeze-frames?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 17, how many learners were secure on “Book-wide synthesis”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “Which oral poets had a public role in Turkish culture (Dede Korkut, Karacaoğlan, aşıklar at weddings)?” in Chapter 11, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 13 did you hear (*making them to cry · *a large group leading by the tribal leaders · Not only … without but also · So used to start a new topic instead of a conclusion)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Can learners limit a generalisation with Despite / However / according to, as Chapter 10 does with women's experiences?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 10 transfer task, count learners who limit their claim with one of the chapter's markers.
Recycle: in Chapters 14 and 17, ask learners to rewrite one 'all' or 'none' sentence as a limited claim.
Check: after the B2 End-of-Level Test, note item 17 (Despite + noun phrase) for the class in Score a test, and read the writing papers for limited claims.
Decide: list the markers learners use most and least, and plan one practice for the least used.

collaboration: Share your counts for despite + noun phrase with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 8 lesson on Hilf al-Fudul with the social studies teacher, and link it to how citizens ask for their rights today.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: A City and an Age
objectives: I can explain why the writer describes two empires before turning to Mecca.
I can define the Age of Ignorance by its place and time.
I can move from a broad context to a precise local focus in my own writing.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Put five sentences from the opening in the writer’s order, using reference words and the transition signal, then correct three forms: “which we now call Istanbul” (no extra it), because + clause rather than because of, and an era “that covers” a period (not who). The last activity asks you to frame a historical introduction of your own.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: SU-per-pow-ers, RI-val-ry, rev-e-LA-tion, CON-quest. Read the long first sentence without the brackets first, then read it again with them in a lower voice.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Middle Ages”. Which two dates frame the period? Listen once and follow the zoom: world, region, city. Read again and mark every reference word (these, the time, that time) with what it points back to.
discussionPoints: Two superpowers exhausted each other while Arabia had no political unity. Why might a divided region be affected by powers far beyond its borders?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Middle Ages” and “Mecca”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find the sentence that begins “After describing …”. Ask what the writer does before it and after it. Choose the option that describes that move, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short introduction to a different historical place. Start with the wider world, name one pressure or rivalry, then narrow to your place and period with a clear transition sentence.

content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match five sentences with what the writer is doing (correcting an assumption, holding two beliefs together, reporting a view, showing surprise, stating certainty), then choose “when”, “who” and “were placed”. The last activity asks you to explain a religious contradiction.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: LAT, ma-NAT, UZ-za. Stress: i-DOL-a-trous, ME-di-a-tors, res-ur-REC-tion. Give each stance word its own pause: “Actually, …”, “Oddly enough …”, “No doubt, …”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Allah and the Idols”. What role did the idols have? Listen once for the main parts of religious life. Read again and mark each stance word and the attitude it shows.
discussionPoints: The Arabs believed Allah was the creator and still worshipped idols. Why do people sometimes act against what they themselves believe?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Idolatry” and “Allah and the Idols”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read the sentence with “Although” and the sentence with “were seen as”. Choose the option that keeps both ideas, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe the beliefs of a different group or period in five sentences. Include one belief that seems to clash with another, report people’s views with “were seen as”, and show your own stance with one marker.

whatToNotice: The chapter describes a system with contradictions: Belief in Allah as creator, worship of idols, no belief in the Afterlife, reliance on omens.
Notice “Idols were seen as go-betweens (mediators).” “Were seen as” reports the people’s view, not the writer’s.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Allah and the Idols”. What role did the idols have?
Listen once for the main parts of religious life.
Read again and mark each stance word and the attitude it shows.
Open the picture hotspots “Idolatry” and “Allah and the Idols” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the number of idols, three names and who the Hanifs were.
Paragraph 2: find what the Arabs believed about Allah and what they did not believe.
Paragraphs 3–4: find the most common form of worship and how people made decisions.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: idolatrous, Hanifs, mediators, Resurrection, omens.
“Before doing anything, people sought omens.” What does this show about how people made decisions?
Write one sentence with mediators and one with omens.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question is about how people saw their idols. Paragraph 2 gives the answer in two short sentences.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read the sentence with “Although” and the sentence with “were seen as”.
Choose the option that keeps both ideas, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the role of the idols?
Can I name two stance words and what they show?
Can I explain why “were seen as” is not the writer’s own view?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Describe the beliefs of a different group or period in five sentences. Include one belief that seems to clash with another, report people’s views with “were seen as”, and show your own stance with one marker.

content.chapter: Chapter 13: Islam and a New Society
objectives: I can explain why a religious message affected political and economic power.
I can compare two reactions to the Qur’an.
I can pack and unpack sentences with participle clauses and “as well as”.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the job of “So” (drawing a conclusion), then rewrite three sentences: “this made them cry”, “Not only … but also the respect they received from other tribes”, and “a large group that was led by the tribal leaders”. The last activity asks you to explain how a change in one area affects another.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: in-ter-con-NECT-ed, op-po-SI-tion, au-THOR-i-ty, pres-TI-gious, PROPH-et-hood. Read the long participle sentence in paragraph 3 with a pause at each comma.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “New Community”. What made this community different? Listen once for the principle and the two reactions. Read paragraph 3 again and mark the two groups and their reactions.
discussionPoints: The same message touched some hearts and was denied by others. What makes people open or closed to an idea that challenges them?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Opposition” and “New Community”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Read the sentence that starts with “So”. Decide whether the writer presents the opposition as expected, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how one new idea in a different school, society or period affected politics, money or status. Start with a general principle, then draw a conclusion with So.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from a general principle (three interconnected areas) to Mecca’s leaders and then to the first listeners.
Notice “So, it is understandable that Islam faced opposition”. “So” draws a conclusion; “understandable” means predictable, not justified.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “New Community”. What made this community different?
Listen once for the principle and the two reactions.
Read paragraph 3 again and mark the two groups and their reactions.
Open the picture hotspots “Opposition” and “New Community” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the three areas and the conclusion drawn from them.
Paragraph 2: find two sources of the Quraysh’s leadership and what they wanted to protect.
Paragraph 3: find how the message changed those who accepted it and how the large group reacted.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: interconnected, opposition, authority, prestigious, prophethood.
“They were serving as the prestigious caretakers of the pilgrimage in the Arabian Peninsula.” What would the leaders lose if this role changed?
Write one sentence with authority and one with interconnected.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about the writer’s view in paragraph 1. Read the three opening sentences together.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Read the sentence that starts with “So”.
Decide whether the writer presents the opposition as expected, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why religion affected power?
Can I describe both reactions to the Qur’an?
Can I unpack “making them cry”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how one new idea in a different school, society or period affected politics, money or status. Start with a general principle, then draw a conclusion with So.

objectives: I can explain who the first Muslims were and who opposed them.
I can explain elite opposition without reducing it to wealth alone.
I can use quantity words and ranges accurately.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four expressions with what they tell you precisely (a range, almost no one, many, in the first few years), then correct “almost none of”, “whose survival” and an Although sentence without “but”. The last activity asks you to write a qualified analysis of power.
content.pronunciationFocus: Numbers: Between five thousand and ten thousand; forty-six people. Stress: RAD-i-cal, LAW-ful, su-PE-ri-or, PROM-i-nent. Read the quotation “Trade is like usury” as the Quraysh’s own words.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “First Muslims”. Who were many of them? Listen once for the groups in the chapter. Read again and circle every quantity word (between, almost no one, many, almost none).
discussionPoints: The Qur’an called people to be fair to the poor, pay zakat and give alms. What would change in a town if its richest people took this seriously?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “First Muslims” and “Power”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 4. Read “The new belief system was introducing radical changes in every area.” Ask what the quotation is an example of, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Analyse why a powerful group in a different place resisted change. Give an economic reason, a status reason and one qualified exception, and keep every number and group word accurate.

whatToNotice: The chapter is precise with numbers and groups: between 5,000 and 10,000 people, 46 early Muslims, almost no one from the super-rich, many of the poor.
Notice “Although the leading figures of the Quraysh were not always extremely wealthy”. The writer adds an exception so the claim is not only about money.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “First Muslims”. Who were many of them?
Listen once for the groups in the chapter.
Read again and circle every quantity word (between, almost no one, many, almost none).
Open the picture hotspots “First Muslims” and “Power” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the population of Mecca, the number of early Muslims and who many of them were.
Paragraphs 2–3: find why the upper class opposed the new formation and the example of Abu Talib.
Paragraphs 4–5: find what the Quraysh said about usury and what the leaders said about Muhammad (pbuh).
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: super-rich, formation, radical, lawful, leadership position.
“The new belief system was introducing radical changes in every area.” Which radical change does the writer give as an example?
Write one sentence with radical and one with lawful.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the writer quotes “Trade is like usury”. Read the sentence just before the quotation.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 4.
Read “The new belief system was introducing radical changes in every area.”
Ask what the quotation is an example of, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I describe the first Muslims accurately?
Can I explain the opposition with more than one reason?
Can I explain the difference between “almost none” and “none”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Analyse why a powerful group in a different place resisted change. Give an economic reason, a status reason and one qualified exception, and keep every number and group word accurate.

content.chapter: Chapter 15: Opposition to the New Faith
objectives: I can trace how the opposition grew step by step.
I can explain who suffered the most and why.
I can use “would” for a future seen from the past.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Put four moments in order using At first, However, when … and went further, then choose “would”, “where” and “who”. The last activity asks you to explain why pressure grew and who paid the highest cost.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: bi-LAL, u-MAY-ya. Stress: MON-o-the-ism, ex-ploi-TA-tion, BOY-cott, star-VA-tion. Read the dates as “six seventeen to six twenty”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Boycott”. What is a boycott? Listen once. Paragraph 3 describes cruelty; read it calmly. Read again and mark At first, However, when and went further.
discussionPoints: The Prophet (pbuh), Khadija and Abu Talib spent all their wealth to support the Muslims. What does it cost to stand by people under pressure?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Bilal” and “Boycott”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Read the “However, when …” sentence to its end. Choose the option that names the cause, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how pressure grew in a different situation. Use at least three stage signals and say who was most exposed to harm and why.

whatToNotice: The opposition escalates: mockery, fierce opposition, torture of the weak, then a social and economic boycott.

Notice “They knew that the Prophet’s call to monotheism … would eventually bring them face to face with people who carried out these practices.” “Would” shows what the leaders expected, seen from the past.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Boycott”. What is a boycott?
Listen once. Paragraph 3 describes cruelty; read it calmly.
Read again and mark At first, However, when and went further.
Open the picture hotspots “Bilal” and “Boycott” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the call to monotheism rejected.
Paragraphs 2–3: find how the leaders mocked the Prophet (pbuh) and what turned mockery into fierce opposition.
Paragraphs 3–4: find what Umayya did to Bilal, when the boycott took place and who spent their wealth.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: monotheism, exploitation, mock, boycott, starvation.
“Poor people or those without powerful protectors suffered the most.” Why did protection matter so much?
Write one sentence with exploitation and one with boycott.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what turned mockery into fierce opposition. Read the sentence that begins with “However, when”.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Read the “However, when …” sentence to its end.
Choose the option that names the cause, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name the stages of the opposition?
Can I explain why the poor suffered the most?
Can I explain “would eventually bring”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how pressure grew in a different situation. Use at least three stage signals and say who was most exposed to harm and why.

objectives: I can explain the religious, economic and moral reasons for the Quraysh’s hostility.
I can explain why freedom of choice could not work at that time.
I can use hypothetical conditions and “Otherwise” correctly.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose the meaning of “Otherwise” (if he did step outside his tribe’s views), then correct “if they lost”, “they would be judged” and “Because of this”. The last activity asks you to analyse a choice that social pressure limited.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: hos-TIL-i-ty, a-BAN-don, fa-NAT-i-cism, STATE-less. Read “Otherwise, he would be left unprotected” with a clear pause after Otherwise.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Tribal Fanaticism”. How is it different from ordinary loyalty? Listen once and count the reasons for hostility. Read paragraph 4 again and mark “Otherwise” and what it refers to.
discussionPoints: Leaving the tribe meant losing all protection. What makes it hard today to disagree with your own group, and what helps people do it fairly?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Idols” and “Tribal Fanaticism”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 4. Read the sentence with “Otherwise” and the final sentence of the chapter. Decide whether the statement matches them, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Analyse a situation in a different setting where people were free to choose in theory but not in practice. Use one hypothetical condition, “Otherwise”, and one cause with “Because of this”.

whatToNotice: The chapter gives several reasons in turn: the old religions, wealth from idols, fear of judgment, and tribal fanaticism.
Notice “in today’s terms, means being stateless and being left defenseless.” The writer uses a modern analogy to show the cost of leaving the tribe.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Tribal Fanaticism”. How is it different from ordinary loyalty?
Listen once and count the reasons for hostility.
Read paragraph 4 again and mark “Otherwise” and what it refers to.
Open the picture hotspots “Idols” and “Tribal Fanaticism” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the two main reasons for the Quraysh’s hostility.
Paragraphs 2–3: find what the leaders would lose and what they refused to believe.
Paragraph 4: find what happened to a member who stepped outside his tribe’s views and why freedom of choice could not work.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: hostility, abandon, afterlife, tribal fanaticism, stateless.
“A tribal member could not show the courage to step outside the views of his tribe.” Why was courage not enough?
Write one sentence with abandon and one with stateless.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement links freedom of choice with tribal protection. Check the last paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 4.
Read the sentence with “Otherwise” and the final sentence of the chapter.
Decide whether the statement matches them, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I give three reasons for the hostility?
Can I explain the stateless analogy?
Can I correct “if they would lose”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Analyse a situation in a different setting where people were free to choose in theory but not in practice. Use one hypothetical condition, “Otherwise”, and one cause with “Because of this”.

objectives: I can explain the book’s final contrast between Islam and Jahiliyyah.
I can tell the leaders’ accusation from the writer’s view.
I can separate historical evidence from a modern analogy.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match five sentences with what the writer is doing (two meanings, every group, the other side, past and future, present and past), then report the leaders’ words (“he had destroyed their unity”) and identify Abu Jahl with “who was”. The last activity asks you to connect history and the present without mixing them up.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: DREAD-ful, op-PRES-sion, im-mo-RAL-i-ty, AR-ro-gance. Read the list “slaves, women, poor, or the weak” slowly, giving each group the same weight.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Human Honor”. What sits at the heart of Islam, according to the chapter? Listen once for the final message of the book. Read again and mark the leaders’ words, the writer’s claims and the modern comparison.
discussionPoints: Whether they are slaves, women, poor or weak, the chapter says, they all deserve respect. Where will you practise this idea this week?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Human Honor” and “Against Ignorance”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one item at a time. Find the paragraph where it appears and read that sentence again. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short conclusion about the whole book. Keep three parts separate: What happened in seventh-century Mecca, the wider idea, and one careful comparison with today.

whatToNotice: The chapter widens the term: Jahiliyyah is a period in the past and also a way of thinking that can still exist today.
Notice “The dreadful situation in the twenty-first century reminds us of the dark period of ignorance in seventh-century Mecca.” This is an analogy the writer draws, not historical evidence.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Human Honor”. What sits at the heart of Islam, according to the chapter?
Listen once for the final message of the book.
Read again and mark the leaders’ words, the writer’s claims and the modern comparison.
Open the picture hotspots “Human Honor” and “Against Ignorance” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.

Paragraph 2: find what is at the heart of Islam and which groups deserve respect.
Paragraphs 3–4: find the two meanings of the term and what Islam has always done.

“The term both refers to pre-Islamic Arabia and also describes any culture, society or way of thinking that comes from human arrogance.” Why does arrogance connect the two meanings?
Write one sentence with human honor and one with arrogance.

Find the paragraph where it appears and read that sentence again.
Match again.

Can I report the leaders’ accusation as theirs, not the writer’s?
Can I say which sentence is an analogy?

metadata.title: Mecca B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Judge • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study Mecca Before Islam on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the argument of the 17 chapters.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Tell sources and facts from the writer’s interpretation.
Use qualified language when the evidence is qualified.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text, not with guesses.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 17.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One person or group in the book I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 17 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1: A clear plan helps you keep going and see your progress.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one personal goal for this book, for example a skill you want to improve.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week. Short, spaced reviews help you remember.
Before Chapter 1, answer the “I can” statements in section 10, “Look Back”. Answer them again when you finish.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the argument.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the argument, once to follow the exact wording.
points: First listening: What is the writer claiming?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence and read it with the same pauses and stress.

sections.title: 4. Evidence or Interpretation?
sections.text: This book mixes facts, sources and the writer’s own judgments. Learn to tell them apart.
points: A source has a reference, such as a surah or a hadith collection.
A figure can be checked: dates, numbers, places.
A judgment evaluates: “It can be said that …”, “This number shows us …”, “mostly”.
Keep your own claims as careful as the evidence.

sections.title: 5. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five or six Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to work out the meaning yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Use the word in a sentence that explains a cause or a contrast.

sections.title: 6. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Answer the Quick Challenge before reading the feedback. Then do the three Language Focus activities.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): See what a sentence does in the argument.
Activity 2 (Build): choose, correct or rewrite forms from the chapter.
Activity 3 (Use): Write a short B2 response about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph at a time.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Separate facts from judgments in two colors.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book contrasts the Jahiliyyah with justice, mercy and human dignity. Connect each value to one action.
points: Justice: Protect people with no power (Chapter 8).
Fair wealth: Honest trade instead of usury, and help for the poor (Chapters 7, 14).
Right loyalty: Do not defend a group when it is wrong (Chapters 10, 16).
Equal dignity: Every human being deserves respect (Chapter 17).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 17, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these statements before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge: not yet, partly or yes. They come from the CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) for level B2. One book is one step towards them, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can read for pleasure with a large degree of independence, adapting style and speed of reading to different texts, using appropriate reference sources selectively.”
Speaking: “I can describe the personal significance of events and experiences in detail.”
Writing: “I can give a review of a film, book or play.”

Mediation: “I can convey detailed information and arguments reliably, e.g. the significant point(s) contained in complex but well-structured texts within my fields of professional, academic and personal interest.”
Which study steps helped me most in this book, and why?
What was hard, and which strategy did I use?
What will I change in my plan for the next book?
